official_skills.notes: Uses the agentskillsforall CLI, not the skills CLI.

The repository README states it is a skill SOURCE repository, not installed directly; distribution happens through per-client plugins. Confirm the current install route before recommending a command. There is no per-SDK repository such as sentry-nestjs-sdk.

gap_map.why_it_matters: No NestJS-team skill collection was found on 2026-08-27. Community collections exist but none is canonical, so recommending one would push a stranger's opinions into every future decision on the project.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor works from the codebase and from NestJS documentation on demand, and states plainly that no framework-team skill is available for this stack.

gap_map.why_it_matters: Nest's DI container makes it trivial to mock everything, which produces suites that pass while the wiring is broken. Someone has to decide which seams are real and which mocks are lies.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor applies references/quality-gate.md, and requires at least one test per feature that exercises the real module wiring.

gap_map.why_it_matters: Guards and interceptors are easy to add and easy to forget. An endpoint with no guard looks identical to one that is intentionally public.
gap_map.fallback: The mentor requires every new controller route to declare its authorization decision explicitly, including 'public on purpose'.

layers.name: unit
layers.belongs_here: a provider's business rules with collaborators supplied directly
layers.does_not_belong_here: anything needing the DI container to prove it
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: the test builds a TestingModule to call one pure method

layers.name: integration
layers.belongs_here: real module wiring via Test.createTestingModule, overriding only what leaves the process
layers.signal_you_picked_wrong: every provider is overridden - the test now asserts the mocks

layers.name: e2e
layers.belongs_here: the HTTP surface end to end against a running app

testing.proportions: NestJS team: pragmatic - real module wiring where valuable, mocking where appropriate. They provide useMocker for classes with many dependencies, noting it exists because mocking them all takes a long time - itself a signal the class has too many.
rules: At least one test per feature exercises the real module wiring. Nest makes mocking everything trivial, and a fully mocked suite passes while DI is broken.
Override at the boundary, not at every provider. overrideProvider is for what leaves the process.
Globally registered guards, interceptors and pipes are not exercised by a narrow unit test - cover them where they actually run.
resolve() returns an instance from its own DI sub-tree, so two calls give different instances. Comparing references there will mislead you.
traps: A fully mocked TestingModule stays green while the real provider graph is broken - the most common false-confidence failure in this stack.
Request-scoped providers behave differently under test; a singleton assumption passes locally and leaks state in production.
Global guards do not run in a narrow TestingModule, so an endpoint tested in isolation appears authorized when it is not.
Validation pipes are global by default: a DTO test that skips the pipe proves nothing about what the endpoint accepts.
what_not_to_test: That Nest injects dependencies, or that a decorator registers a route.
DTO classes with no logic beyond decorators.
testing.notes: The Nest CLI scaffolds test, test:e2e and test:cov scripts. Read package.json before assuming they exist - projects rename them.

growth_thresholds.extract_shared_module: >=2 feature modules import the same provider
growth_thresholds.split_module: a module declares more than 10 providers

layers.name: Controller
layers.holds: transport: parsing, DTO validation, shaping the response
layers.must_not: hold business rules - a controller method past 30 lines has absorbed the service

layers.name: Service / provider
layers.must_not: know about HTTP - no Request, no Response, no status codes

layers.name: Module
layers.holds: the wiring: what a feature provides and what it exports
layers.must_not: export everything - every export is a contract with the rest of the app

variants.name: Feature modules only
variants.cost: boundaries are conventions; an over-eager exports list dissolves them

variants.name: Feature modules plus a domain layer
variants.use_when: the same rules serve HTTP and a queue consumer
variants.cost: more indirection; premature here is the over-abstraction signal

rules: A controller does transport only. Business rules live in a provider.
A service never imports Request or Response. If it needs the caller's identity, pass it as an argument.
A module exports only what another module actually imports.
Cross-feature access goes through an exported provider, never into another feature's internals.
Global providers (APP_GUARD and friends) are invisible at the call site - list them in CLAUDE.md or nobody will know they run.
architecture.notes: Nest is opinionated about modules and DI and unopinionated about where business rules live, which is exactly where projects drift.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Nest defines controllers, providers and modules but takes no position on what belongs in a provider versus a dedicated domain object.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Rules in services until the same rules serve a second entry point.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: Rules that end up in controllers cannot be reused by a queue consumer or a cron job without copying them.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Singleton, request-scoped and transient behave very differently and the choice is invisible at the call site.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Singleton. Reach for request scope only when per-request state genuinely cannot be an argument.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A singleton holding request state leaks one user's data into another's response.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Nest bundles no ORM, and where a transaction begins and ends is not decided for you.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: Decide the transaction boundary at the same time as the ORM, not later.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A transaction boundary discovered late means partial writes already reached production.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: Guards can be global, per-controller or per-route, and mixing them puts the answer in two places.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: An endpoint that looks guarded because a sibling is guarded is how public endpoints ship.

key_decisions.why_it_is_forced: ConfigModule is optional and process.env works, so config access spreads unless a decision is made.
key_decisions.reasonable_default: ConfigModule with schema validation - it fails at boot rather than at the first request.
key_decisions.cost_of_getting_it_wrong: A missing variable found at runtime is an outage; found at boot it is a failed deploy.

operability.observability: Nest ships a Logger with a replaceable implementation, and an exception filter is the single place an unhandled error can be captured before it becomes a 500 with no record.
operability.authorization: Guards. A globally registered guard is invisible at the call site, so the strategy must be written down or a reader cannot tell a public route from an unguarded one.
done_checks: clean install from a fresh clone
rules: Every controller route states its authorization decision, including 'public on purpose'.
Every outbound call states a timeout and a retry count including zero.
An exception filter reports unhandled errors somewhere a human sees them. Without it a 500 leaves no trace.
Configuration is validated at boot. A missing variable should fail the deploy, not the first request.
Nothing request-scoped is stored on a singleton provider.

dead_code_risks: Providers resolved by injection token or by string, never imported by class
Guards, interceptors, pipes and filters applied via decorators or APP_GUARD-style global providers
DTO classes referenced only through decorator metadata
Entities discovered by an ORM glob pattern rather than by import
Controllers whose only inbound reference is the HTTP router
